title: Shloka 121
subtitle: The slight smile, and the teacher's form

namas.gloss: Whose Long Eyes Sway A Little
namas.translation: Her long eyes rock very slightly from side to side, the small restless motion of a gaze that misses nothing.

compound.gloss: she whose long eyes are gently swaying

namas.gloss: Whose Face Shines With A Faint Smile
namas.translation: The barest trace of a smile breaks on her lips and lights her whole face from within.

compound.gloss: she whose face is lit up by a slight smile

namas.translation: She takes shape as the teacher, so that whoever gives genuine instruction is wearing her form for the moment.

compound.gloss: the embodied form of the guru

namas.translation: Every good quality is laid up in her the way coin is laid up in a strongroom.

children.gloss: a store, a hoard, a treasury

namas.translation: She is the mother of the herds, the source of the cattle on whose milk and labour human life has always leaned.
Guha, the war-god reared in secret, has his origin in her.

compound.gloss: the place where Guha was born

children.gloss: Guha, the god Skanda, reared in a hidden place
ground, the place where a thing comes to be

commentary.meaning: Six names, and the verse breaks cleanly in half. The first line stays on her face and says two very small things about it: her long eyes are swaying slightly, her mouth is lit by the slightest of smiles. Both names open with dara, a little, and the repetition is the point — the poet declines the large gesture twice in a row. The second line abandons description altogether for four flat predications, and all four open with the same guttural: she is the form the teacher takes, the treasury in which good qualities are stored, the mother of cattle, the ground out of which Guha was born. Nothing in the second line can be looked at. The movement across the two lines is from the face a worshipper sees to the offices she holds in the world — instruction, wealth, sustenance, offspring — and the hinge between them is the smile. A gaze that keeps shifting and a mouth that has just begun to open are exactly the condition of someone about to speak, and the first thing the second line names is the teacher.
commentary.history:
The word dara is the least conspicuous thing in the verse and the most carefully chosen. As the first member of a compound it means slightly, a little, barely — and classical poetry uses it constantly to mark something that has not yet fully arrived: daravikasita of a bud half open, daravilupta of a thing nearly effaced. Sanskrit has a graded vocabulary for laughter, from smita, the closed-lip smile, up through hasita and vihasita to aṭṭahāsa, the roaring laugh that Śākta literature gives to Kālī and to Bhairava in the cremation ground. This verse takes the quietest term on that scale and then damps it further with dara. What makes the name interesting is the verb attached to it: ujjvalat is the present participle of ud-√jval, to flare up, to blaze out. The smallest possible smile is given the strongest possible verb of light, and the disproportion is the whole content of the name.

Āndolita, in the first name, is the past participle of ā-√dul, to set swinging; āndolā is a swing, the kind hung from a branch, and the word survives in the Hindi and Marathi hindolā. Her long eyes are not darting; they are rocking, with the slow return of something suspended. Long eyes are a fixed convention of Indian description — eyes said to reach almost to the ears, compared to lotus petals or to fish — and the convention on its own would be unremarkable. The addition of a slight swaying turns a static feature into a gesture, and it is the gesture of a gaze that is taking in more than one thing.

Guru, the first word of the second line, is an ordinary adjective before it is a title: heavy, weighty, and in prosody a long syllable, the exact counterpart of laghu, light. It is cognate with Greek barys and Latin gravis. Alongside this plain etymology the tradition preserves a nirvacana, an interpretive word-splitting, which the Advayatāraka Upaniṣad states and the later Guru Gītā repeats: gu stands for darkness and ru for what removes it. In Śrīvidyā the guru is not an optional convenience. The fifteen-syllabled vidyā is transmitted, not acquired, and the ritual manuals have the practitioner worship the lineage of teachers — conventionally in three streams, the divine, the perfected and the human — before touching the worship of the goddess herself. Mūrti, from √mūrch, means a form that has solidified, and the name says something stronger than that she resembles the teacher: whoever is genuinely teaching is, for that duration, her congealed shape.

Nidhi is a hoard, specifically treasure buried in the ground, of the sort Kubera keeps; guṇa is first of all a strand of a rope, and only then a quality or a virtue. Both senses are live here. Read morally, the name says every good quality is deposited in her. Read through Sāṃkhya, where the three guṇas — sattva, rajas and tamas — are the three strands twisted together into the whole of unconscious nature, it says she is the store from which those strands are paid out. The commentators generally take the moral reading as primary and let the technical one stand behind it.

Go is one of the widest words in the language. It is a cow or an ox, and by extension the herd that constituted movable wealth in the Vedic economy; it is also a ray of light, which is why the sun is gopati; it is the earth; and it is the organ of sense, which is why the field of a sense faculty is its gocara. Mother of cattle is therefore the surface of the name and not its limit, and commentators generally allow the wider senses, so that she becomes the mother of the rays and of the senses that catch them. Behind the literal reading stands Surabhi, also called Kāmadhenu, the wish-granting cow drawn up in the churning of the ocean, whose descendants are the cattle of the world.

Guha is Skanda, the son born to Śiva and Pārvatī for one purpose, to lead the divine army against the demon Tāraka, whom no one already alive could kill. In the version Kālidāsa tells in the Kumārasambhava and the Purāṇas tell at greater length, Śiva's seed proved unbearable, passed through Agni, and was set down at last in a thicket of reeds — śara-vaṇa, from which he is Śaravaṇabhava — where the six Kṛttikās, the Pleiades, nursed the child, giving him six faces and the name Kārttikeya. Guha itself means the hidden one, from guhā, a cave or hiding place, and the name registers that he was born and reared out of sight. That same word guhā is the standard Upaniṣadic term for the cavity of the heart where the self is said to be lodged, and the ambiguity is not lost on readers of the hymn: the birthplace of Guha is also the ground of what is born in the cave. The name matters more in the South, where Skanda as Murugan has an independent and much older cult than the Sanskrit sources suggest, and this hymn is a South Indian text.
commentary.practice:
The verse is a regular anuṣṭubh, four feet of eight syllables, and the count is easy to verify: da-rā-ndo-li-ta-dī-rghā-kṣī, then da-ra-hā-so-jjva-la-nmu-khī. The break falls after the sixteenth syllable, at the end of the second name, which is also where the verse changes subject. Breathe there.

The two names of the first line begin identically and then diverge at the third syllable, and this is where reciters slip. Darāndolita has a long ā, because dara has combined with āndolita and short a plus long ā yields long ā; darahāsa keeps the short a of dara and puts the length on hāsa instead. Fix the difference by hearing it as darā- against dara-hā-, and the two will not collide.

Three clusters in the first line need separate attention. In āndolita the nd is dental throughout: the n closed at the teeth, the d released from the same position, with no intrusive vowel. In dīrghākṣī the rgh is a retroflex r followed by an aspirated velar — one sound with breath in it, not g plus h — and the kṣ that follows is the familiar velar-plus-retroflex-sibilant. Hardest is ujjvalat, where jj is a genuine double consonant: hold the first j closed and release the second, then let the v follow. English will want to reduce the whole cluster to a single j sound, and the metre will notice.

The second line runs four names together with two visarga sandhis. Gurumūrtiḥ and guṇanidhiḥ both end in visarga, and before the voiced consonant that follows each becomes r: gurumūrtir guṇanidhir gomātā. The final visarga of guhajanmabhūḥ, closing the verse, is a genuine breath after the long ū and should be sounded, faintly echoing the vowel before it.

For recitation as archanā, where each name is spoken in the dative followed by namaḥ, this verse is unusually instructive, because its six names use four different declensions. The two ī-stems of the first line take -yai: darāndolitadīrghākṣyai, darahāsojjvalanmukhyai. The two i-stems take -aye: gurumūrtaye, guṇanidhaye. Gomātā is an ṛ-stem and gives gomātre. Guhajanmabhūḥ is a ū-stem and gives guhajanmabhuve. A student who can produce all six from the nominatives has most of the noun system of the nāmāvalī in hand.

As for what the verse asks of the person chanting it: the first line trains attention downward, onto a movement almost too small to see and an expression that has barely formed. It is a corrective to the scale of the surrounding hymn, which has been dealing in cosmic offices for many verses. The second line then restores that scale, but by way of the teacher rather than the cosmos — which is to say that the route from the small thing observed to the large thing believed runs through a person who taught you.

crossReferences.deva: शिवे शृङ्गारार्द्रा तदितरजने कुत्सनपरा सरोषा गङ्गायां गिरिशचरिते विस्मयवती । हराहिभ्यो भीता सरसिरुहसौभाग्यजयिनी सखीषु स्मेरा ते मयि जननि दृष्टिः सकरुणा ॥
crossReferences.iast: śive śṛṅgārārdrā taditarajane kutsanaparā saroṣā gaṅgāyāṃ giriśacarite vismayavatī | harāhibhyo bhītā sarasiruhasaubhāgyajayinī sakhīṣu smerā te mayi janani dṛṣṭiḥ sakaruṇā ||
crossReferences.translation: Wet with love when it falls on Śiva, full of disdain for everyone else, angry at the Ganges, astonished at the doings of the mountain's lord, frightened of the snakes he wears, outdoing the loveliness of the lotus, smiling among her companions — and, mother, merciful when it falls on me: such is your glance.
crossReferences.relevance: The classic treatment of her eyes as a moving thing rather than a feature, and the best gloss available on what a slightly swaying gaze is for. The verse runs the aesthetic list of rasas through a single glance, each shift produced by what the eye happens to land on, which is precisely the restlessness that darāndolitadīrghākṣī records. The last word of the verse also supplies the affective register in which the sahasranāma's slight smile should be taken. Editions differ over sarasiruhasaubhāgyajayinī and the variant reading jananī; the sense of the rasa-list favours jayinī.

crossReferences.deva: यस्य देवे परा भक्तिर्यथा देवे तथा गुरौ । तस्यैते कथिता ह्यर्थाः प्रकाशन्ते महात्मनः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yasya deve parā bhaktir yathā deve tathā gurau | tasyaite kathitā hy arthāḥ prakāśante mahātmanaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: These matters, when they have been spoken, become clear only to the great-souled one who has the highest devotion toward god, and toward the teacher as toward god.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest scriptural statement of the equation that gurumūrtiḥ compresses into a single word, and the verse the initiatory traditions cite when they insist that the teaching cannot be had from a book. Note the direction of the identification: the Upaniṣad asks the student to regard the teacher as god, while the sahasranāma makes the stronger claim from the other side, that the goddess is the form the teacher is wearing.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library, repr. Chowkhamba)
references.note: The only complete English window onto the eighteenth-century commentary that most later expositions quietly follow. The translation is Victorian and often obscure, and Bhāskararāya's derivations are frequently more ingenious than probable, but for names like gomātā, where the whole question is how far the semantic range of go may be pushed, it shows you what a traditional pandit thought the licence was.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Look up go and read the entry to the end. Cow, ox, herd, ray, the earth, water, speech, the organ of sense, a singer, the number nine — the sheer spread is the reason gomātā cannot be settled by translation alone, and no commentary will make the point as efficiently as three columns of citations.

references.title: Kumārasambhava
references.author: Kālidāsa; tr. Hank Heifetz as The Origin of the Young God (University of California Press, 1985)
references.note: The literary source for Guha's birth, and the reason the episode is remembered as poetry rather than as mythology. Heifetz translates the eight cantos generally accepted as Kālidāsa's and his notes are honest about where the received text stops being his. Read cantos one and five for Pārvatī's austerities before returning to guhajanmabhūḥ.

references.title: The Many Faces of Murukaṉ: The History and Meaning of a South Indian God
references.author: Fred W. Clothey (Mouton, 1978)
references.note: Essential for seeing that Guha is not simply a Sanskrit deity who travelled south. Clothey traces the Tamil god of the hills and his absorption into the Skanda of the Purāṇas, which explains why a South Indian hymn to the goddess should think a name for his birthplace worth spending a quarter of a verse on.

references.title: Auspicious Wisdom: The Texts and Traditions of Śrīvidyā Śākta Tantrism in South India
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: Useful here for its account of initiation and the guru lineages, which is what gurumūrtiḥ presupposes. Brooks is good on the social fact that this is a tradition of transmission rather than of texts, and on how the three streams of teachers are actually invoked in practice.
